paper_name: Workload assignment for global real-time scheduling on unrelated multicore platforms
paper_description: This paper introduces a new hierarchical platform model for unrelated multicore systems and proposes workload assignment methods to improve schedulability by minimizing inter-cluster migrations. It presents a Linear Programming (LP) formulation that acts as an exact feasibility test and discusses its relationship to existing LP models. The paper also explores a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approach to minimize task presences on clusters, aiming to reduce migration overhead.

formal_description.statement: A cluster \pi_k is faster than cluster \pi_l if for all tasks \tau_i (1 <= i <= n), r_{i,k} >= r_{i,l}.

variables.r_i_k: processing rate of task i on cluster k
variables.r_i_l: processing rate of task i on cluster l

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a relative speed ordering between clusters for all tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: Cluster A is faster than Cluster B if every task runs at least as fast on A as it does on B.
steps: For each task tau_i, compare its execution rate on cluster pi_k (r_i_k) with its rate on cluster pi_l (r_i_l).
If r_i_k is greater than or equal to r_i_l for ALL tasks tau_i, then cluster pi_k is faster than cluster pi_l.
key_insights: This definition establishes a consistent ordering of cluster speeds.

formal_description.statement: \pi_k is defined to be the fastest processor if k is the smallest index such that for all 1 <= l <= m, \pi_k >= \pi_l. Wlog (by reordering the clusters) we can assume that \pi_1 is the fastest cluster.
formal_description.conclusion: Identifies the fastest cluster in the platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: The fastest cluster is the one that is faster than or equal to all other clusters, and it's the first one in the ordered list.
steps: Assume clusters are ordered such that pi_1 is the fastest, pi_2 is the second fastest, and so on.
The fastest cluster (pi_1) is the one that satisfies the condition of Definition 2.1 against all other clusters (pi_2 to pi_m).
key_insights: Simplifies analysis by designating a reference fastest cluster.

formal_description.statement: The utilization of a task \tau_i is u_i = C_i / T_i.

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i on a fictional core

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fraction of processor time a task requires.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the proportion of a single processor's time that task i would need if it were the only task running.
steps: Take the worst-case execution time (C_i) of task i.
Divide it by the period (T_i) at which task i releases new jobs.
The result (u_i) is the task's utilization.

formal_description.statement: A task \tau_i has a presence on a cluster \pi_h if x_{i,h} > 0. The number of presences Pr_i corresponds to the number of times where \tau_i has a presence in a cluster: Pr_i = |{x_{i,h} > 0 | h = 1, ..., m}|.

variables.x_i_h: fraction of processing capacity of a core in cluster pi_h assigned to task tau_i
variables.Pr_i: number of presences of task i on clusters

formal_description.conclusion: Quantifies how many distinct clusters a task is assigned to.

informal_sketch.intuition: A 'presence' means a task is assigned some processing time on a cluster. The number of presences is simply how many different clusters a task is assigned to.
steps: For a given task tau_i, examine its assignment values x_{i,h} for all clusters pi_h.
Count how many of these x_{i,h} values are greater than zero.
This count is the number of presences (Pr_i) for task tau_i.
key_insights: Directly relates to the potential for inter-cluster migrations.

formal_description.statement: A task \tau_i will have to migrate between clusters if, and only if, Pr_i > 1. Therefore, any presence greater than one is a presence in excess that will generate at least one inter-cluster migration.

variables.Pr_i: number of presences of task i on clusters

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for a task requiring inter-cluster migration.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task is assigned to more than one cluster (Pr_i > 1), it means it needs to move between clusters, which incurs cost.
steps: Calculate the number of presences (Pr_i) for task tau_i.
If Pr_i is greater than 1, then the task has an 'excess presence'.
Each excess presence implies at least one inter-cluster migration is needed.
key_insights: Directly links task assignment to migration cost.

formal_description.statement: A system is feasible on the platform if, and only if, LP-Cluster has a solution. Proof: (i) if there is no solution to the LP, then the system is not feasible. This will occur if Equation 2 or Equation 3 are not satisfied. In the first case, there would be at least one task \tau_i such that sum(x_{i,h} for h=1 to m) > 1. It means that \tau_i must be executed in parallel which is forbidden in our model of sequential tasks. In the second case, a cluster \pi_h would need a processing capacity higher than its total capacity m_h. Now we prove that (ii) finding a solution to this LP problem guarantees that the system is feasible. The proof sketch is depicted in Figure 2. The cluster workload assignment matrix X is of dimension n x m. Indeed, by construction of the LP problem, it has n rows with a sum of coefficients less than one, and m columns with a sum of coefficients less than m_h, h = 1, ..., m. First, we replace each column h, corresponding to the task assignment to cluster \pi_h by m_h columns, one for each core, such that the sum of the coefficients on each of the columns is not greater than one. For the sake of the proof, we simply consider, on each row i of the new columns k = 1, ..., m_h, m_h, such that the total capacity fraction allocated to each task on each cluster is evenly distributed on each of its cores. In this manner, we obtain a workload assignment matrix on the cores X_c of dimension n x M, where M = sum(m_h for h=1 to m) is the total number of cores. On each column, m_h represents the capacity fraction of core \pi_{h,k} allocated to task \tau_i. By construction, since originally the used capacity of cluster \pi_h to tasks was sum(x_{i,h} for i=1 to n) <= m_h, we have on each column for pi_j k, sum(x'_{i,h_k} for i=1 to n) <= 1. From this cluster cores workload assignment matrix, we can easily create a bistochastic matrix B of size (n + M) x (n + M), as done in [23]. A bistochastic (or doubly stochastic) matrix is a square matrix of non-negative real numbers, having each of its rows and columns summing to 1. Formally, for all i = 1, ..., n: sum(B_{i,h} for h=1 to n+M) = 1 and for all h = 1, ..., M: sum(B_{i,h} for i=1 to n+M) = 1. B is constructed as follows: B_{i,h_k} = x'_{i,h_k} for i=1..n, h_k=1..M. B_{i,n+j} = delta_i for i=1..n, j=1..n where delta_i is the laxity of the task tau_i, i.e. the fraction of time during which tau_i is left idle. B_{h_k, h_k} = 1 - sum(x'_{i,h_k} for i=1 to n) for h_k=1..M. B_{h_k, n+j} = 0 for h_k=1..M, j=1..n. B_{n+i, h_k} = 0 for i=1..n, h_k=1..M. B_{n+i, n+j} = delta_i if i=j else 0. The diagonal coefficients of B_n correspond to the laxity of the task tau_i, i.e. the fraction of time during which tau_i is left idle. B_M is a M x M diagonal matrix, such that B_M(h_k, h_k) = 1 - sum(x'_{i,h_k} for i=1 to n) for all h_k. The diagonal coefficients of B_M correspond to the slack of the core pi_{h_k}, i.e. the fraction of time during which pi_{h_k} is left idle. X_c is the transpose of the core workload assignment matrix X_c, and has a dimension M x n. By construction, we obtain a square bistochastic matrix B of dimension (n +M) x (n +M) expressing the fraction of each core that has to be allocated to each task, as well as the slack of the cores and the laxity of the tasks. Following the Birkhoff-von Neumann (BvN) theorem, such a matrix can be decomposed into a convex combination of permutation matrices [23], where delta_i is a real coefficient in (0, 1], sum(delta_i for i=1 to k) = 1, and P_i is a permutation matrix. A permutation matrix is a binary square matrix where there is exactly one 1 on each row and each column. This can be seen as a matching between tasks (rows) and cores (columns). Indeed, one and only one coefficient P_i(h, k) = 1 means that task on column k will be assigned to the core of the row h for a duration delta_i. The assignment matrix X_c states that assigning a ratio of x'_i,h_k of core pi_{h_k} to task tau_i during each of its periods ensures that its jobs will be completed. However, we need to ensure that a job is never executed on two different clusters at the same time. For each time window [t_1, t_k), between two successive releases at times t_1 and t_k (or deadlines since tasks have implicit deadlines), we can use the BvN decomposition to create such a schedule. We use the matching P_1 on the time window [t_1, delta_1 * (t_k - t_1)), by definition of a permutation matrix, this matching ensures that a task is assigned to at most one core in this time windows. Similarly, we can use the following permutation matrices obtained in the BvN decomposition, each permutation matrix P_i covering a sub-interval of duration delta_i * (t_k - t_1). Since by the BvN theorem, sum(delta_i for i=1 to k) = 1, we can completely schedule every task on the interval [t_1, t_k), ensuring that a task is never executed on more than one core at the same time. This one time unit schedule can then be stretched to fit into intervals of time delimited by successive task release dates. This technique is also referred to as deadline partitioning [25].

variables.LP-Cluster: Linear Programming formulation for cluster workload assignment
variables.x_i_h: fraction of processing capacity of a core in cluster pi_h assigned to task tau_i
variables.m_h: number of cores in cluster pi_h
variables.M: total number of cores (sum of m_h)

assumptions: preemptions and migrations are performed at no extra cost
formal_description.conclusion: The existence of a solution to the LP-Cluster formulation is a necessary and sufficient condition for the schedulability of the task set on the given platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: If we can find a valid way to distribute task workloads across clusters (satisfying capacity and task demand constraints), then a schedule exists where all tasks meet their deadlines. Conversely, if no such distribution is possible, the system is not schedulable.
steps: Formulate the workload assignment as a Linear Program (LP-Cluster) with constraints ensuring: (1) each task receives its required processing capacity from clusters, (2) no task is assigned more than 100% of its capacity across all clusters, and (3) no cluster is overloaded.
If LP-Cluster has a feasible solution (i.e., all constraints can be satisfied), then the system is schedulable.

The proof involves transforming the cluster assignment into a core assignment, then into a bistochastic matrix, which by the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem can be decomposed into a sum of permutation matrices. Each permutation matrix represents a valid schedule for a time slice, and by combining these, a complete feasible schedule can be constructed.

If LP-Cluster has no solution, it means either a task requires more than 100% of its capacity (constraint 2 violated) or a cluster is asked to provide more capacity than it has (constraint 3 violated), making the system unschedulable.
key_insights: The LP formulation captures all necessary conditions for schedulability. The Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem provides a constructive proof of schedulability from a valid LP solution.

formal_description.statement: The condition sum(x_{i,h} for h=1 to m) <= 1 for all tasks tau_i ensures that a task is not executed in parallel on multiple cores.

variables.x_i_h: fraction of processing capacity of a core in cluster pi_h assigned to task tau_i

formal_description.conclusion: Prevents a task from being assigned more than its total required processing capacity.

informal_sketch.intuition: If the total fraction of processing time assigned to a task across all clusters is 1 or less, it means the task is not being asked to run on multiple cores simultaneously.
steps: Consider a task tau_i.
Sum up the fractions of processing capacity assigned to tau_i from all clusters (x_{i,1} + x_{i,2} + ... + x_{i,m}).

If this sum is less than or equal to 1, it implies that the task's total assigned workload does not exceed what a single core can provide over time, thus preventing parallel execution of the task itself.
key_insights: This constraint directly enforces the sequential execution model of tasks.

formal_description.statement: The condition sum(x_{i,h} for i=1 to n) <= m_h for all clusters pi_h ensures that a cluster is not overloaded.

variables.x_i_h: fraction of processing capacity of a core in cluster pi_h assigned to task tau_i
variables.m_h: number of cores in cluster pi_h

formal_description.conclusion: Ensures that the total processing demand placed on a cluster does not exceed its available capacity.

informal_sketch.intuition: If the total processing time assigned to all tasks within a single cluster is less than or equal to the total processing power of that cluster (number of cores * 100% capacity), then the cluster can handle the load.
steps: Consider a cluster pi_h.
Sum up the fractions of processing capacity assigned to all tasks (tau_1 to tau_n) on this specific cluster (x_{1,h} + x_{2,h} + ... + x_{n,h}).
If this sum is less than or equal to the number of cores in the cluster (m_h), it means the cluster's total capacity is not exceeded.
key_insights: This constraint ensures that the platform's resources are not over-committed at the cluster level.

formal_description.statement: The problem of deciding if there is a BvN decomposition of a given doubly stochastic matrix with k permutation matrices is NP-complete in the strong sense.
formal_description.conclusion: Determining the minimum number of scheduling decisions (represented by permutation matrices) is computationally hard.

informal_sketch.intuition: Finding the absolute minimum number of distinct scheduling configurations (permutation matrices) needed to represent a workload distribution is a very difficult problem, likely requiring exponential time in the worst case.
steps: Consider a doubly stochastic matrix (representing workload distribution).
The goal is to decompose this matrix into a sum of permutation matrices, each weighted by a coefficient.
The theorem states that deciding if such a decomposition exists with a specific, small number (k) of permutation matrices is NP-complete in the strong sense.
This implies that minimizing k (and thus minimizing scheduling decisions/migrations) is NP-hard.
key_insights: The complexity of minimizing scheduling decisions (and thus migrations) is inherent and not easily solvable efficiently.

formal_description.statement: The condition \ell <= 1 in LP-CFeas constrains solutions of LP-CFeas to be solutions of LP-Cluster.

variables.LP-CFeas: LP formulation for clustered systems minimizing makespan
variables.LP-Cluster: LP formulation for cluster workload assignment

formal_description.conclusion: Solutions of LP-CFeas with \ell <= 1 satisfy the feasibility constraints of LP-Cluster.

informal_sketch.intuition: The LP-CFeas formulation, when aiming for a makespan of 1 or less, effectively enforces the same core constraints as LP-Cluster.
steps: LP-CFeas has constraints: sum(x_{i,h} * r_{i,h}) = u_i, sum(x_{i,h}) <= ell, sum(x_{i,h}) <= m_h * ell.
LP-Cluster has constraints: sum(x_{i,h} * r_{i,h}) = u_i, sum(x_{i,h}) <= 1, sum(x_{i,h}) <= m_h.
If ell <= 1 in LP-CFeas, then sum(x_{i,h}) <= ell implies sum(x_{i,h}) <= 1 (matching LP-Cluster constraint 2).
Also, if ell <= 1, then m_h * ell <= m_h, so sum(x_{i,h}) <= m_h * ell implies sum(x_{i,h}) <= m_h (matching LP-Cluster constraint 3).
key_insights: The makespan objective in LP-CFeas, when bounded by 1, implicitly enforces the total capacity constraints of LP-Cluster.
